# Course Information & Logistics {.unnumbered}

::: {.callout-important}
**This page describes how the course is structured, not when things
happen this year.** Specific dates, deadlines, room numbers, and
this year's teaching-staff names live in Canvas (and, eventually, a
proper per-year scheduling system this book will link to) — not here.
Nothing on this page should need editing just because a new year's
calendar or staffing changed.
:::

## Goals

Four threads, running through the whole course: biological databases and
the basic tools built on them; neural networks and deep learning, hands
on; recent machine-learning methods for protein structure prediction; and
a capstone project — see [Capstone](capstone.qmd) — that applies all of
it to secondary structure prediction.

## People

The course has two teachers — one covering the machine-learning half, one
covering classical bioinformatics — and several teaching assistants (TAs)
who run the lab sessions. Who's teaching in any given year is a Canvas
matter, not a book matter; a handful of pages later in this book do credit
a specific person's own lecture material by name (Petras Kundrotas's
decks are cited that way on several days) — that's a separate, deliberate
citation, not the same thing as this page's staffing description.

## How grading works

- **Project: 30% of the final grade** (see [Capstone](capstone.qmd)) —
  needs at least 40% on its own to count toward passing.
- **Exam: 70% of the final grade** — also needs at least 40% on its own.
- **Both together need to reach 50%** to pass the course overall.
- The exam is **in person, on paper**, with a stated limit on how many
  pages of personal notes you're allowed to bring (check the current
  year's exam announcement for the exact number).
- If you fail the exam but passed everything else, a re-exam is normally
  offered; if you already passed (grade E or higher), there's no retake
  just to try for a better grade.

## Lab quizzes

Each day with a lab (see the [Course Schedule](schedule.qmd)) has a short
online lab-report quiz, graded pass/fail against a **50% correct**
threshold. A few things about how these work, unchanged from year to
year:

- **Mandatory** — every lab quiz needs to be passed, not just attempted.
- **Same deadline for every lab** in a given run of the course, rather
  than one deadline per lab — check Canvas for what that date actually
  is this year.
- **Available as soon as published** — you don't have to wait for the
  matching lecture to start a lab quiz if it's already up.
- **One redo chance** if you fail — normally only at the *next* time the
  course runs, and the lab itself may have changed by then, so passing it
  the first time is worth the effort.
- You may discuss *methods and approaches* with your peers, but the
  actual answer you submit needs to be your own.

## Lectures: come prepared

Every lecture has an **at-home preparation part** before you show up —
in this rebuilt book, that's literally what each day's own on-page
"Check your understanding" quiz widget and pre-lecture discussion
notebooks are for (see `CONTRIBUTING.md`'s authoring recipe if you're
looking at how these get built, not just how to use them). **Lectures are
not recorded** — past experience is that recording lectures measurably
reduces how many students actually show up, which defeats a course this
interactive.

## Coding environment

- **Visual Studio Code** is the recommended editor, but any editor you're
  comfortable with works.
- Most labs run fine on your own laptop. A few need a shared course
  server instead — for those, you'll be asked to generate a public SSH
  key and send it in, so it can be added to the server's authorized
  keys.
- For anything that needs a GPU, **Google Colab** is the recommended
  fallback (every notebook in this book has a "Open in Colab" badge for
  this reason) — it's free up to some usage limits, needs a
  Google account, and disconnects a session left idle too long, so don't
  leave one open and walk away.
- **PyMOL** is the recommended protein-structure viewer for the
  structure-focused labs (Day 7's lab already assumes you have it
  installed) — it's free for students and runs on most platforms. If you
  don't have a computer that can run it, ask early rather than the day
  of the lab.

## Plagiarism

This has been a real problem in past years, not a hypothetical one. If
you signed a plagiarism-policy form for this course, that's the actual
policy in force — read it. Discussing approaches with classmates is
fine and expected (see the lab-quiz note above); submitting someone
else's actual answers as your own is not. If you're ever unsure where
that line is on a specific assignment, ask before submitting, not after.
